name: Aristotle
info: Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath, born in Stagira, who founded the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum in Athens and whose works contain the earliest known systematic study of logic.

facts.born: 384 BCE in Stagira, Chalcidice, in northern Greece; son of Nicomachus, personal physician to King Amyntas of Macedon, and Phaestis, whose family came from Chalcis in Euboea
facts.died: 322 BCE at Chalcis, Euboea, of natural causes, after fleeing Athens when he was reportedly denounced for impiety
facts.role: Philosopher and polymath; member of Plato's Academy in Athens for nearly twenty years (to 348/47 BCE); tutor to Alexander, son of Philip II of Macedon (from 343/42 BCE); founder and head of the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum, Athens, for twelve years (from about 335 BCE)
facts.known: the earliest known systematic study of logic; founding the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum; tutoring Alexander the Great; the first systematic study of biology; the four causes and the theory of matter and form; the Nicomachean Ethics, Politics and Poetics

t: A physician's son from Stagira, Aristotle spent nearly twenty years at Plato's Academy, tutored the young Alexander of Macedon, and then founded his own school in the Lyceum in Athens.

His surviving treatises, generally thought to be lecture aids rather than works for publication, cover logic, metaphysics, physics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetry; only around a third of what he wrote survives.

His logic remained dominant in the West until the 19th century and his physical science was not replaced systematically until the Enlightenment, and writers from Maimonides to Bertrand Russell have by turns revered and attacked him.
dyk: Aristotle described the hectocotyl arm that cephalopods use in sexual reproduction; his description was widely disbelieved until the 19th century.
ev: Born in Stagira, Chalcidice, the son of Nicomachus, physician to King Amyntas of Macedon, and Phaestis
Leaves Athens after Plato's death, having spent nearly twenty years at the Academy, and goes with Xenocrates to Assos in Asia Minor
Invited to Pella by Philip II of Macedon to tutor his thirteen-year-old son Alexander
Back in Athens, rents the Lyceum and establishes his own school there, later known as the Peripatetic school
Reportedly denounced for impiety by Demophilus and Eurymedon the Hierophant, he flees Athens for his mother's family estate at Chalcis
Dies at Chalcis, Euboea, of natural causes, leaving his works to Theophrastus, his successor as head of the Lyceum

sections.early:
Aristotle was born in 384 BCE in Stagira, in Chalcidice, about 55 km east of modern Thessaloniki. His father, Nicomachus, was the personal physician of King Amyntas of Macedon; his mother, Phaestis, had origins in Chalcis on Euboea. Nicomachus was said to have belonged to the medical guild of the Asclepiadae and was likely responsible for his son's early interest in biology and medicine. Ancient tradition held that the family descended from the legendary physician Asclepius and his son Machaon.

The details of his life are not well established: the biographies written in antiquity are often speculative, and historians agree only on a few salient points. Both parents died while he was still young, and Proxenus of Atarneus became his guardian. Little information about his childhood survives, but he probably spent some time in the Macedonian capital, Pella, where he made his first connections with the Macedonian monarchy.

At the age of seventeen or eighteen he moved to Athens to continue his education at Plato's Academy. There he became distinguished as a researcher and lecturer, and his tutor Plato nicknamed him the "mind of the school". He probably experienced the Eleusinian Mysteries, of whose sights he wrote that "to experience is to learn". He remained in Athens for nearly twenty years, leaving only after Plato's death.
sections.rise:
Aristotle left Athens in 348/47 BCE, after Plato's death. The traditional story records that he was disappointed with the Academy's direction once control passed to Plato's nephew Speusippus, though anti-Macedonian sentiment in Athens may also have influenced him. With Xenocrates he went to Assos in Asia Minor at the invitation of a former fellow student, Hermias of Atarneus, and stayed for a few years. At Assos, and later on the nearby island of Lesbos, he and his colleague Theophrastus carried out extensive research in botany and marine biology. During this time he married Pythias, the adoptive daughter and niece of Hermias.

In 343/42 BCE Philip II of Macedon invited him to Pella as tutor to his thirteen-year-old son Alexander, a choice perhaps influenced by his family's ties to the Macedonian dynasty. He taught at the private school of Mieza, on the royal estate near Pella; the lessons probably included ethics and politics as well as Euripides and Homer, and he gave Alexander an annotated copy of the Iliad. The tutorship probably lasted only a few years, since at about sixteen Alexander was appointed regent of Macedon.

A year after Philip's assassination in 336 BCE, Aristotle returned to Athens for the second and final time. As a metic he could not own property there, so he rented a building known as the Lyceum and established his own school in it. Its colonnade, the peripatos, gave the school the name Peripatetic.
sections.deeds:
Aristotle conducted courses and research at the Lyceum for twelve years, lecturing to small groups and, with students such as Theophrastus, Eudemus and Aristoxenus, building a large library of manuscripts, maps and museum objects. Between 335 and 323 BCE he is believed to have composed many of his works. The dialogues he wrote survive only in fragments; the surviving treatises, among them the Physics, Metaphysics, Nicomachean Ethics, Politics, On the Soul and Poetics, are generally thought to be lecture aids for his students.

With the Prior Analytics he is credited with the earliest systematic study of logic. In the Metaphysics he concluded that a particular substance is a combination of matter and form, a theory called hylomorphism, and he distinguished four causes: material, formal, efficient and final. He was the first person to study biology systematically: he spent two years observing the zoology of Lesbos and the surrounding seas and distinguished about 500 animal species, drawing on his own observations, on beekeepers and fishermen, and on travellers' accounts.

In ethics he taught that the aim of deliberate human action is eudaimonia, generally translated as "happiness", which requires good character and the virtuous mean between excess and deficiency. In the Politics he treated the city as a natural community and stated that "man is by nature a political animal". The Rhetoric sets out three kinds of appeal, ethos, pathos and logos, and the Poetics describes tragedy as an imitation of action arousing pity and fear.
sections.opponents:
Aristotle's philosophy took shape partly against that of his teacher. Where Plato held that universals exist separately from the things that participate in them, Aristotle maintained that they are encountered only when instantiated in particular things, and in On the Soul he criticised Plato's theory of the soul; 20th-century scholarship held that he had there misinterpreted Plato. He was rather critical of democracy, and his attitude towards Persia was strongly ethnocentric: in one famous example he counsels Alexander to be "a leader to the Greeks and a despot to the barbarians".

His science was corrected from antiquity onwards. Archimedes corrected his theory that bodies move towards their natural resting places, and Herophilus of Chalcedon placed intelligence in the brain rather than, as Aristotle had, in the heart. John Philoponus and Galileo are said to have shown by experiment that a heavier object does not fall faster than a lighter one; Carlo Rovelli argues to the contrary that Aristotle's physics of motion is correct within its domain, that of bodies falling through a fluid such as air.

Modern critics have been sharper. Bertrand Russell claimed that "almost every serious intellectual advance has had to begin with an attack on some Aristotelian doctrine" and called his ethics "repulsive". In 1985 the biologist Peter Medawar wrote of a "farrago of hearsay, imperfect observation, wishful thinking and credulity". Zoologists have frequently mocked his errors, although modern observation has confirmed several of his more surprising claims.
sections.last:
During his years at the Lyceum his wife Pythias died, and Aristotle became involved with Herpyllis of Stagira; they had a son, whom he named Nicomachus after his father. Alexander had deeply admired him, but near the end of the king's life the two became estranged, holding diverging opinions on the administration of city-states, the treatment of conquered populations such as the Persians, and philosophical questions. A widespread speculation in antiquity held that Aristotle played a role in Alexander's death; the only evidence is an unlikely claim made some six years afterwards.

Alexander's death rekindled anti-Macedonian sentiment in Athens. In 322 BCE Demophilus and Eurymedon the Hierophant reportedly denounced Aristotle for impiety, and he fled to his mother's family estate at Chalcis on Euboea. He was said to have remarked, "I will not allow the Athenians to sin twice against philosophy", a reference to the trial and execution of Socrates. He died at Chalcis of natural causes later that year, having named his student Antipater as his chief executor and asked in his will to be buried next to his wife.

He left his works to Theophrastus, his successor as head of the Lyceum, who passed them to Neleus of Scepsis in Asia Minor; there the papers remained hidden until the collector Apellicon bought them. Copies of the major works were meanwhile circulating in Athens, Alexandria and later Rome. Only around a third of his original output survives.
sections.legacy:
The Lyceum grew into the Peripatetic school, and the surviving treatises were compiled in the 1st century BCE by Andronicus of Rhodes. Commentary became the chief way of engaging with them, from Boethus of Sidon to Alexander of Aphrodisias, and the Neoplatonists made his logical and physical works an introduction to Plato. After the pagan schools were closed by order of Justinian in 529, Byzantine study of him was primarily from a Christian perspective.

His works were revived in the Abbasid Caliphate, where most were translated into Arabic and taken up by Al-Kindi, Al-Farabi, Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and Averroes; medieval Muslim scholars called him the "First Teacher". Moses Maimonides based his Guide for the Perplexed on Aristotelianism. In the Latin West he was practically unknown from c. 600 to c. 1100 except through Boethius's translation of the Organon; translations from Arabic and Greek in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries revived interest, and Thomas Aquinas called him "The Philosopher".

His conception of logic was dominant in the West until 19th-century advances in mathematical logic, and his physical science was not replaced systematically until the Enlightenment. Charles Darwin wrote in 1882 that Linnaeus and Cuvier "were mere schoolboys to old Aristotle". His ethics has gained renewed interest with modern virtue ethics, and Niko Tinbergen's four questions about animal behaviour are based on his four causes. Jonathan Barnes wrote that "an account of Aristotle's intellectual afterlife would be little less than a history of European thought".

summary: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), born in Stagira, studied at Plato's Academy, tutored Alexander of Macedon and founded the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum in Athens. His treatises on logic, nature, ethics and politics shaped medieval Islamic, Jewish and Christian scholarship, and his logic and physics held their place into modern times.

notes: The article writes BC; BCE used here as in the guide's examples.

Dates differ inside the article: the lead has him leave the Academy c. 347 BC and tutor Alexander 'beginning in 343 BC'; the Life section says 348/47 BC and 343/42 BC. The events use the lead's single years (no slash dates in ev); the sections and role give the Life section's double years.

Event '335 BCE' for the founding of the school: the article says he returned 'a year after Philip II's assassination in 336 BC' and dates the Athens period 'between 335 and 323 BC'; it gives no explicit year for renting the Lyceum.
No year is given for his arrival at the Academy (only 'at the age of seventeen or eighteen'), nor for Alexander's death, so neither is an event.

The lead says his father died when he was a child and the Life section that both parents died young; the section follows the Life section. The lead also says he left the Academy 'at the age of thirty seven'; not used.
The nickname 'mind of the school' is stated flatly by the article ('by his tutor Plato'); kept flat.

'On kingship' and 'On behalf of the Colonies' (scholars speculate), the Organon's six books, the psychology of memory and dreams, economics, and the eponyms (Aristotle Mountains, crater, asteroid) were left out for space.

Russell's 'repulsive' and Medawar's words are quoted from the article; Medawar is trimmed (the article's full phrase begins 'a strange and generally speaking rather tiresome farrago' and ends 'credulity amounting to downright gullibility').
The two 322 BCE events share a year; the article says he died 'later that same year'.
